chapters.title: Chapter 2: Working Capital and the Cash Conversion Cycle

lessons.title: Negative Working Capital: How Some Indian Companies Get Paid Before They Pay

children.text: Everything so far has assumed the business funds the gap. Konkan Ceramics pays for clay on Day 52 and gets paid on Day 151, and somebody has to bridge those 99 days. But a whole category of businesses runs the loop backwards. They collect from customers first and pay suppliers later, so the gap funds them instead. Their customers and suppliers supply the working capital, and the business gets to use that money for free.

body.text: A negative cash conversion cycle means the business is funded by other people's money. Customers pay before delivery, or suppliers wait long after it. Either way, growth generates cash instead of consuming it.

children.text: The Same Formula, the Other Side of Zero
Nothing new is needed. Take the formula from Lesson 2.2 and let the last term get large enough.

body.caption: If suppliers wait longer than your stock and your customers combined, you are running on their money

body.title: Two ways to end up on the right side of zero

columns.label: Collect early
points: Retail and restaurants: paid in cash or by UPI at the counter
Subscriptions and SaaS billed annually in advance
Gyms, coaching classes and schools collecting fees upfront
Airlines and hotels taking bookings months ahead
Any business asking for an advance with the purchase order

columns.label: Pay late
points: Large FMCG companies with 150-day supplier terms
E-commerce marketplaces settling sellers after a delay
Buyers with enough scale to dictate terms to smaller vendors
Businesses using letters of credit or channel finance to stretch payment
Anyone whose stock sells faster than their supplier credit runs out

body.text: The second column has a legal boundary in India. Stretching payment to a micro or small supplier beyond the MSMED Act limit is not a working capital strategy, it carries interest and a tax consequence. The companies below achieve long payable days with large suppliers, on agreed terms, which is a different thing entirely. Lesson 3.2 covers the line.

children.text: Two Real Companies, Two Opposite Choices
These are consolidated figures from screener.in for the year ended March 2026. Both businesses are admired for operational discipline. Their cycles look nothing alike.

body.caption: Cash conversion cycle, year ended March 2026 (days, as reported on screener.in)

body.title: Where the days sit: HUL vs DMart, year ended March 2026

body.label: HUL's cash conversion cycle
body.context: From screener.in, year ended March 2026. Stock moves in 61 days, distributors pay in 19, and suppliers are paid in 169. HUL therefore holds roughly 89 days of free funding from its supply chain, and that funding grows automatically as the business grows.

children.text: Now look at DMart, and resist the assumption that a positive number means worse management. DMart pays its suppliers in about 8 days. That is a deliberate trade: pay fast, and demand the lowest possible purchase price in return. Those lower purchase costs are the foundation of its everyday low pricing. It funds 37 days of stock out of its own pocket and collects from shoppers on the spot, at 1 debtor day.

body.text: This is the most important idea in the lesson. Supplier credit is not free, it is priced into what you pay for goods. HUL uses its scale to take the credit. DMart uses its scale to take a discount instead. Both are rational. Anyone who tells you a negative cycle is automatically better has not asked what the credit cost in margin.

body.title: Cross the zero line
body.prompt: A packaged foods company holds 40 days of inventory, collects from distributors in 10 days, and pays its suppliers in 75 days. What is its cash conversion cycle, in days? Enter a negative number if it is negative.
body.explanation: 40 plus 10 minus 75 is minus 25 days. The company sells the stock and collects the money 25 days before its own suppliers have to be paid. Every rupee of extra sales hands it more cash to hold, which is why fast-growing businesses with this shape rarely need working capital loans.

children.text: Float: Getting Paid Before You Deliver
The other route to a negative cycle is collecting in advance. Sunrise Fitness is a fictional three-branch gym chain in Hyderabad with 2,000 members paying ₹12,000 a year upfront.

body.caption: Sunrise Fitness: the economics of collecting first

cells: Trainers, rent, electricity and equipment servicing, about ₹16 lakh a month
Members are on average halfway through their year

stats.label: Float held
stats.context: Cash in the bank, service not yet delivered

stats.label: Compared with profit
stats.context: The float is bigger than two years of profit

stats.label: Interest avoided at 11%
stats.context: What borrowing that ₹1.2 crore would have cost

children.text: The owner can open a fourth branch costing ₹1 crore without approaching a bank. That is the power of float. It is also where the trouble starts, because that ₹1.2 crore is not profit and it is not really his.

body.caption: Accountants call the balance deferred revenue, and it sits on the balance sheet as a liability

body.title: Why advance money is a liability, not income

children.text: When a member pays ₹12,000 in April, the gym has not earned ₹12,000. It has promised twelve months of service. Revenue is recognised as the months pass, and until then the unearned part sits as a liability, usually called deferred revenue or advance from customers.
Month 1:
₹1,000 recognised as revenue, ₹11,000 still a liability.
Month 6:
₹6,000 recognised, ₹6,000 still owed as service.
If the member cancels or the gym shuts:
the unearned balance is a genuine obligation, refundable in many cases.

There is a tax wrinkle too. For services, GST is generally payable when the advance is received, so a slice of the float goes to the government long before the service is delivered. For goods, tax is instead due on the invoice. Confirm the current position with your chartered accountant before relying on it.

In real estate the law goes much further. Under the RERA rules, a developer must keep a large majority of the money collected from buyers, 70% in the standard provision, in a separate project account, precisely to stop advances from one project funding another.

body.text: Float feels like wealth and behaves like debt. It is spent most easily in exactly the situation where it is least safe to spend: when growth is slowing and the owner is looking for cash. If renewals at Sunrise Fitness fall by 20%, roughly ₹24 lakh of float disappears while rent and trainer salaries carry on unchanged.

body.title: What the balance sheet calls it
body.textWithBlank: Money collected from a customer before the service is delivered is recorded as a ___ on the balance sheet, not as revenue.
body.explanation: Until the service is delivered, the business owes it. Recognising the full amount as revenue on the day it is collected overstates profit and, far more dangerously, makes the owner feel richer than the business actually is.

children.text: When the Model Bites Back
A negative cycle is a wonderful thing while a business is growing and a brutal one when it stops. The mechanism is symmetrical, and most managers only discover the second half the hard way.

body.caption: The same model, growing and shrinking

cells: Cash pours in ahead of costs
Collections and supplier credit both rise before the bills come due
Money coming in matches obligations falling due
Collections shrink immediately while yesterday's supplier bills and service obligations still have to be honoured
Terms are cut from 90 days to advance payment exactly when the business can least afford it

body.text: This is why a negative cycle is a reason to hold more cash, not less. The businesses that get hurt are the ones that treated float as spare money and put it into new branches, new inventory or a new office, and then met one bad quarter.

body.title: Which one is most likely to run negative?
body.question: Which of these Indian businesses is most likely to operate with a negative cash conversion cycle?
options: A capital goods maker supplying transformers to state electricity boards on 120-day terms
A pharmaceutical exporter holding large batch inventories
A cinema chain selling tickets and food for cash or UPI, and paying distributors and vendors weeks later
A tile manufacturer selling to builders on 75-day credit
body.explanation: The cinema collects at the point of sale, holds almost no inventory beyond snacks, and settles distributors and vendors afterwards. The other three all carry long inventory or long receivables, and supply customers who are slower to pay than their own suppliers are to be paid. Government and infrastructure buyers in particular are famous for stretching payment.

body.title: Switch the customers to annual upfront billing
body.scenario: You run finance at a Bengaluru software company with 400 business customers paying ₹5,000 a month, billed monthly in arrears and collected in about 45 days. The CEO wants to offer two months free to anyone who switches to annual upfront payment, expecting most customers to take it. Sales loves the idea. The board wants your view before the campaign launches.
body.prompt: What is the cash effect, what is the cost, and what would you insist on before approving it?
body.modelAnswer:
The cash effect is large and immediate.
1. Each switching customer pays ten months upfront instead of one month in arrears, collected 45 days later. The working capital swing per customer is close to a year of billing.
2. Across 400 customers at ₹5,000 a month, full adoption would bring in roughly ₹2 crore of cash that currently arrives month by month, and would turn receivables into float.
Now the cost.
3. Two months free is a discount of about 17% on annual revenue. That is expensive money. Compare it with the alternative: borrowing at 11% to 12%, or simply collecting faster.
4. Revenue recognition does not change. Only one month of each annual payment is revenue in that month, and the rest is deferred revenue, a liability. Profit does not jump just because the bank balance does.
5. Churn risk moves. An annual customer who leaves at month three may demand a refund, and refunds come out of cash you have already spent.
What I would insist on.
6. Offer a smaller discount first, one month free, and test it on a segment before the whole base.
7. Ring-fence the cash. Agree in advance that the float funds a defined purpose, not general spending, and report deferred revenue separately every month.
8. Set a refund policy in writing before the campaign, not after the first request.
9. Model a bad case: adoption at 70%, churn doubling in year two, and see whether the business still holds together when the float stops growing.
10. Ask sales whether the same customers would simply pay faster in exchange for a much smaller incentive. Fixing a 45-day collection cycle may deliver most of the benefit at a fraction of the price.

body.title: Find the float in your own business
steps: List every point where your company takes money before delivering: advances, deposits, subscriptions, annual maintenance contracts, booking amounts.
Add up the balance that is collected but not yet earned. That is your float.
Check where it is recorded. If it sits in revenue rather than as a liability, profit is overstated.
Ask what the float is currently funding. Working capital is fine. A new branch or a machine is a maturity mismatch.
Calculate what happens to that balance if sales fall 20% for two quarters.
Check your supplier terms for the same exercise: how much of your funding comes from payables, and how many of those suppliers are micro or small enterprises with statutory payment limits.
Decide a minimum cash buffer you will hold against the float, and write it down before you need it.

cards.definition: Payables days exceed inventory plus receivable days, so suppliers and customers fund the business.
Cash collected before the goods or service is delivered. Usable, but owed.
The accounting name for float. A liability until the service is delivered.
Money taken with the order. The cheapest funding a business can get, and a promise to perform.
Funding a long-term asset with short-term money, such as building a branch out of annual fees.
The margin given up in purchase price in exchange for longer payment terms. Credit is never actually free.

points: A negative cash conversion cycle happens when payable days exceed inventory plus receivable days. Customers and suppliers fund the business.
HUL ran a cycle of minus 89 days in the year to March 2026, with 169 payable days. Growth hands it cash rather than consuming it.
DMart runs a positive 29-day cycle by choice, paying suppliers in about 8 days to buy cheaper. Negative is not automatically better.
Supplier credit is paid for in purchase price. Always ask what longer terms cost in margin.
Float is cash collected but not earned. It is a liability, and treating it as profit is how businesses with full bank accounts fail.
The model reverses when sales fall: collections shrink immediately while obligations continue, so a negative cycle is a reason to hold more cash, not less.

body.text: Sunrise Fitness and the Bengaluru software company are fictional. HUL and DMart figures are consolidated ratios from screener.in as published at the time of writing, and may be restated later. GST treatment of advances and RERA requirements are summarised and can change. Confirm with your chartered accountant. Nothing here is investment advice or a recommendation on any security.
